messages.content: I'm planning a camping trip and I need to know the weather forecast. Can you fetch me the weather data for the campsite located at latitude 35.68 and longitude -121.34 for the next 10 days including daily temperature and precipitation forecasts? Also, I prefer the temperature 2 minute max in Fahrenheit and sum of precipitation in inches.

I’m sorry—I don’t have direct access to live web services or real‑time databases, so I can’t pull up the current 10‑day forecast for your exact location right now. However, you can easily get exactly what you’re looking for yourself! Below is a quick guide on how to retrieve the information using one of the most popular free weather APIs—**Open Meteo**—and how to parse the results into the units you requested. --- ### Step‑by‑step instructions | What | How | |------|-----| | **Get today’s date** | In many programming languages you can just read “today” automatically (`datetime.date.today()` in Python). If doing it manually, note the year/month/day. | | **Build the URL** | ``` https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast? latitude=35.68& longitude=-121.34& daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum& timezone=America/Los_Angeles& start_date={YYYY-MM-DD}& end_date={YYYY-MM-DD} ``` Replace `{YYYY-MM-DD}` with today’s date and ten days later respectively. | | **Units** | By default Open Meteo returns temperatures in Celsius and precipitation in millimetres. Add parameters to convert them:
`temperature_unit=fahrenheit`
`precipitation_unit=inches` | | **Example full URL** | ```https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.68&longitude=-121.34&daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum&timezone=America/Los_Angeles&start_date=2026-05-13&end_date=2026-05-22&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&precipitation_unit=inches``` | > *Tip:* Most browsers will let you paste the link straight into the address bar and see the raw JSON response. --- ### Sample Response Structure Below is a mock snippet showing the kind of JSON you’ll receive once you hit the endpoint. Replace the placeholder values with those returned by the actual API call. ```json { "latitude": 35.68, "longitude": -121.34, "generation_time_ms": 0.5, "utc_offset_seconds": -25200, "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles", "daily_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m_max": "°F", "precipitation_sum": "\"in\"" }, "daily": { "time": [ "2026-05-13", "2026-05-14", "...", "2026-05-22" ], "temperature_2m_max": [72.5, 75.8, ..., 70.2], "precipitation_sum": [0.01, 0.00, ..., 0.12] } } ``` * Each entry under `"time"` corresponds to a calendar day.* * `"temperature_2m_max"` gives the highest temperature recorded during that day (at 2 meters above ground), already converted to °F because of our unit parameter.* * `"precipitation_sum"` shows the total rainfall accumulated that day, expressed in inches.* If you’d like both min/max temperatures, add `temperature_2m_min` to the `daily=` list. And if you truly meant “two‑minute intervals,” you would switch to the `hourly=` option instead, then aggregate the data yourself. --- ### Quick One‑liner (Python) Here’s a minimal script you can run locally (requires `requests`) to print out the same table: ```python import requests, datetime base_url = ("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?" "latitude=35.68&longitude=-121.34&daily=" "temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum&timezone=America/Los_Angeles") dates = [(datetime.datetime.utcnow() + datetime.timedelta(days=i)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d") for i in range(10)] url = f"{base_url}&start_date={dates[0]}&end_date={dates[-1]}" params = {"temperature_unit":"fahrenheit","precipitation_unit":"inches"} resp = requests.get(url, params=params) data = resp.json() print("Date\tMax Temp (°F)\tPrecip (in)") for d,t,p in zip(data["daily"]["time"], data["daily"]["temperature_2m_max"], data["daily"]["precipitation_sum"]): print(f"{d}\t{t:.1f}\t\t{p:.2f}") ``` Run that in any terminal where Python is installed, and you’ll instantly have a neatly formatted table ready for your camp‑planning spreadsheet! --- Let me know if you'd like help tweaking the output further—for instance adding humidity, wind speed, or converting everything back to metric units—or if there's anything else about the trip I can assist with. Happy camping!
